note.happening: Meta rose 3.13% to 628.96. That puts it just above its 200-day average of 626.67 but still well below its 50-day average of 671.34, and the overall trend is still down. No news has come out since the last note, and the next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
note.business: Demand still looks strong. Sales over the past year (trailing twelve months, TTM) are 241.6B, up from 189.5B, and the gross margin is 81.03%. Growth is slowing, though: sales rose 26.07% from a year earlier in the latest quarter, against 33.08% two quarters ago. Margins and cash are where the business is changing. The operating margin (profit from operations as a share of sales) fell to 32.86% from 43.23%. Free cash flow (cash left after running the business and paying for investment) fell to 28.6B from 44.8B. That puts the free-cash-flow margin at only 11.86%. Research spending is 31.68% of revenue. Heavy spending on AI computing has been widely reported (general knowledge) and fits these numbers. The filings flag that profit per share is lagging sales and that last quarter missed forecasts by 29%. The balance sheet is not at risk: debt is 83.7B, cash on hand is 11.2B, available liquidity is 82.4B, and net cash is only -1.2B, a near-even position. Share count rose just 0.04% in a year, so owners are not being diluted. The reported $14.1M of insider selling outside pre-set plans is a sentiment and governance point. It does not change the business. What is at risk is how much cash each dollar of sales turns into. Demand is not at risk.

worth.text: The two valuation methods disagree because they start from different numbers. A DCF (discounted cash flow: today's value of future cash) starts from the shrunken 28.6B of free cash flow and a 9.9% discount rate. It gives 244.22 in the bear case, 379.4 in the base case and 517.42 in the bull case, all below the price. To justify the price, free cash flow would need to start growing at 37.5% a year. Even at 30% starting growth the value is only 477.73. If the operating margin fell to 24%, the value would drop to 245.02. Meta's own price-to-sales history starts from sales, which are still rising. On that measure the stock sits at the 37th percentile of its last five years, with a range of 475.85 to 707.21 to 881.21. Other measures look moderate: the stock trades at 21.5 times trailing earnings and 6.7 times sales, against a peer median of 6.0 times sales. Adjusted for growth, it is roughly in line with peers (1.02). The whole gap comes down to one question: will cash flow return to its old relationship with sales?
